THE SETUP

Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 after the close on Tuesday, November 17. The quarter ended October 25. Guidance is revenue of $108 billion plus or minus 2 percent, gross margin 74 percent plus or minus 50 basis points. Consensus sits at $109.0 billion for revenue and $2.47 for adjusted earnings per share, and it has barely moved in four weeks. The street has not cut this quarter for the governance crisis. The numbers it expects are the numbers the old regime promised.

This is also the first print of the post-Jensen era. Colette Kress runs the call as interim CEO and CFO. The numbers matter. The language matters more. Here is everything worth monitoring, in the order it will arrive.

THE NUMBERS, FIRST 10 MINUTES

- Revenue against the $108 billion guide and the $109.0 billion consensus. A print inside the guide band but below consensus is a miss wearing a beat's clothes. Score it as a miss.
- Data center revenue against $101.8 billion of consensus, and inside it compute against $80.7 billion and networking against $20.0 billion. Networking strong with compute light is mix shift toward systems. Both light is a demand problem.
- The segment cuts by customer type: hyperscale at $53.3 billion of consensus, AI clouds and industrial at $48.9 billion, edge computing at $7.5 billion. The AI clouds line is the neocloud bucket. Its beat or miss is the cleanest read on the demand quality of the ecosystem Nvidi

Ship 42 returned from orbit and was caught by the launch tower arms at Starbase around 4:20 p.m. ET, roughly 22.5 hours after liftoff.

It marks the first time a spacecraft has returned from orbit and been caught by the same tower it launched from.

SpaceX had planned to catch both stages, but the Super Heavy booster was diverted offshore after its catch was aborted.

NVIDIA: LITIGATION HISTORY AND THE SIDE C QUESTION (1/3)

Date: November 14, 2026

Grades used throughout: VERIFIED means a primary document (filing, court order, executed agreement, SEC release) states it. REPORTED means a credible secondary source states it and no primary document was located. NOT FOUND means the searches returned nothing. ESTIMATE means a figure constructed from market benchmarks, labeled as such.

BOTTOM LINE

• Nvidia historically carried entity securities coverage inside a conventional layered D&O tower: its early 2000s tower contained a policy written around securities claims, the entity slot in that era's standard ABC form.
• Nvidia has been sued in four federal securities class actions and has never settled one, so no insurer has ever funded a securities settlement for it, and the absence of such a payment proves nothing about coverage either way.
• Its one documented fight with its D&O carriers was offensive, not defensive: in 2005 Nvidia sued its own carriers when they resisted paying defense costs on the 3dfx creditor claims.
• Today the Financial Times reports a Side A only program, which, if accurate, is a change from Nvidia's own historical posture; the record does not date the change.
• The saving from skipping Sides B and C is on the order of $10M a year (ESTIMATE), about one basis point of Nvidia's roughly $99B of liquidity. It is real money and immaterial at this scale, which is why the absence of entity coverage still needs a reason.

text:
There are two schools of thought on how markets work.

Efficient markets: participants are rational, and all known information is already in the price.

Irrational markets: cognitive biases like overreaction, underreaction, herding, loss aversion and anchoring push prices away from fair value.

Those mispricings persist. Momentum, pre/post-earnings drift, bubbles and crashes all come from them, and limits to arbitrage keep rational traders from fully closing the gap.

There is a pre earnings drift in NVDA and that gap should close prior to earnings. 

That gap is where we do our work.

The obvious question after the Financial Times reported that Nvidia carries up to $900 million of Side A only D&O insurance, with no Side B and no Side C, is why a company of this size would leave its own balance sheet uninsured. The answer being whispered is that the company could not have survived the diligence: that applying for entity coverage would have exposed what was going on inside.

That theory gets the mechanism wrong, and the correct mechanism is more interesting. D&O underwriters do not investigate anybody. What applying for Side B and Side C actually requires is a signature: a set of representations, made after polling the board and the executive team, about what the company and its officers know. The carrier reviews financials, claims history, market capitalization, share volatility, credit spreads, ownership concentration, and litigation history, benchmarks the company against peers, and models securities claim frequency and severity. Most stocks do not go up in a straight line. They go up, they fall apart, and then they go up again — and the fall is where the money is made, if the story is still true.

$PLTR went to $45 in early 2021. Then it fell to $7-8, and the bottom printed near $6. More than an 80% drawdown. Everyone wrote it off. The business kept building — government contracts, then commercial, then AI — and the stock went to $207. Then it fell again, nearly 50%, to about $107. And then it went to $209.

That is the whole lesson. A 50-80% pullback is not always a broken stock. Sometimes it is the same stock, the same story, at a price that makes sense again. The market does not hand out second chances quietly — it hands them out while everyone is busy calling the name dead.
